description: How crime and deviance are socially constructed — varying across time, place and culture.
content_html:
Crime and Deviance: Two Distinct Concepts

One of the first distinctions sociology asks you to make is between crime and deviance. These concepts overlap but are not the same thing. A crime is an act that breaks the formal law; deviance is any behaviour that violates the unwritten social norms of a group or society. Many deviant acts are not criminal — queue-jumping, belching loudly in a restaurant or wearing a swimsuit to a funeral all break social expectations but carry no legal penalty. Equally, some criminal acts are not widely regarded as deviant — many motorists who exceed the speed limit by a small amount do not consider themselves “criminals” in any meaningful social sense.

This distinction matters because sociology treats both crime and deviance as social constructs — they are not fixed, objective categories but are defined and redefined by societies, institutions and individuals over time.

Key Fact

Crime and deviance are related but distinct: crime breaks the formal law; deviance violates social norms. Some acts are only one of these, not both — this distinction is tested directly in your exam.

Formal and Informal Rules

Societies regulate behaviour through two types of rules. Formal rules are codified in law and backed by state sanctions: fines, imprisonment or community service. Informal rules — sometimes called social norms — govern everyday behaviour through informal pressure: social disapproval, ridicule or exclusion from the group. A student who arrives late to every lesson is breaking an informal norm; a student who commits fraud is breaking a formal rule. Both are forms of deviance in the sociological sense, but only the second is a crime.

Societies use sanctions to enforce both types of rules. Positive sanctions reward conformity (a round of applause, a pay rise, social praise); negative sanctions punish deviation (a fine, a prison sentence, social exclusion). The relationship between formal law and informal norms is itself a sociological question: laws tend to reflect the norms of the dominant groups in society, a point Marxist and feminist perspectives challenge.

The Relativity of Deviance

A key insight of sociology is that deviance is relative: what counts as deviant varies across time, place and social situation. The specification explicitly names historical and cultural variations as required content. Three dimensions of relativity are particularly important.

Across time (historical variation): Acts that were once legal can become criminal — fox hunting with dogs was a lawful rural tradition in England and Wales until the Hunting Act 2004 made it a criminal offence. Conversely, acts once treated as crimes can be decriminalised: consensual sexual activity between adult men was a criminal offence in England and Wales until the Sexual Offences Act 1967 partially decriminalised it. The law changes as the values and power structures of society change.

Across place (cultural variation): The same act may be legal in one country but criminal in another. Cannabis possession is permitted for recreational use under certain conditions in the Netherlands but remains a criminal offence in England and Wales. Drinking alcohol in public is unremarkable in most of the United Kingdom but constitutes a serious offence in countries that enforce strict religious law. These cross-cultural variations demonstrate that crime is not an inherent property of an act but a label applied by a society.

Across situation (situational variation): Context shapes whether an act is considered deviant. Killing another person is treated as murder in most contexts but may be regarded as heroic in warfare, or legally permitted as self-defence. A surgeon cutting open a patient’s body with a scalpel is performing a legitimate medical procedure; the same action outside that context would be an assault. Interactionist sociologists like Becker emphasised that deviance is not a quality of the act itself but is created by the reactions of audiences to the act.

A very common examination error is to treat crime and deviance as synonyms. They are overlapping but distinct categories. Think of two overlapping circles: the left circle is all criminal acts, the right circle is all deviant acts. The overlap is acts that are both criminal and widely seen as deviant (violent assault). The left-only region is acts that are criminal but not seen as deviant by most people (minor speeding). The right-only region is acts that are deviant but not criminal (being rude to a stranger). On an exam question asking you to “define deviance”, giving a legal definition will lose marks.

Sociological Perspectives on the Social Construction of Crime

Different sociological perspectives explain the social construction of crime in contrasting ways, reflecting deeper disagreements about the nature of society.

Functionalist perspective: From a functionalist viewpoint, crime and deviance are defined relative to the value consensus of society. Durkheim argued that some level of crime is normal and even functional in any society — it helps clarify the boundaries of acceptable behaviour and, when punished, reaffirms shared values. On this view, defining something as “criminal” is the community expressing its moral boundaries.

Marxist perspective: Marxist sociologists argue that criminal law is not a neutral reflection of shared values but an instrument of class power. The bourgeoisie shape the law to protect their property and interests, criminalising acts common among the working class (street theft) while failing to criminalise or leniently treating harmful acts by the powerful (corporate fraud, tax evasion). The social construction of “crime” therefore reflects and reinforces class inequality.

Feminist perspective: Feminist sociologists point out that laws have historically been made predominantly by men and have often reflected patriarchal interests. Many acts of violence against women — marital rape, for instance — were not defined as criminal in England and Wales until relatively recently (rape within marriage was only conclusively criminalised following the landmark R v R ruling in 1991). Definitions of crime and deviance therefore embed gender power relations.

Interactionist perspective: Interactionists such as Becker argue that no act is inherently criminal or deviant; it becomes so only when a label is successfully applied to it by someone with the power to make the label stick. The social construction of crime is an ongoing process of labelling, negotiation and reaction. Becker used the term moral entrepreneurs to describe individuals and groups who actively campaign for certain behaviours to be defined as deviant or criminal — pressure groups lobbying for new legislation are a contemporary example.

Key Fact

Four perspectives explain social construction differently: functionalists see crime as defined by shared values; Marxists see law as serving the ruling class; feminists see law as historically shaped by patriarchal power; interactionists focus on labelling as the mechanism by which acts become “criminal” or “deviant”.

Law and Morality: Are They the Same?

A final dimension of the social construction of crime is the relationship between law and morality. Not everything that is morally condemned is illegal, and not everything that is illegal is morally condemned by all members of society. Lying to a friend is widely regarded as morally wrong but carries no legal penalty. Some individuals regard civil disobedience — breaking an unjust law — as a moral act. The gap between law and morality varies across time and culture and is itself a product of social processes. Sociologists are interested in who gets to define the law, whose morality it encodes, and whose behaviour it criminalises — questions that run through the entire sociology of crime and deviance.
exam_tip_html: The command word “Define” asks you to provide a clear sociological meaning for a term — not an example of it. Students often write “deviance is when someone does something that breaks the rules, like stealing” and lose a mark because “like stealing” replaces the definition with an example. A strong definition of deviance reads: “behaviour that violates the social norms of a group or society, whether or not it is illegal.” Each mark on a 2-mark Define question typically corresponds to one element of the definition — adding a qualifying clause earns the second mark. On a 12-mark Evaluate question, examiners reward students who present at least two named sociological perspectives in detail and reach a supported judgement that weighs the evidence on both sides. One-sided answers that only present one perspective cannot reach the Mastering tier.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Crime and deviance are distinct: crime breaks formal law; deviance violates social norms. Many acts are only one of these, not both — this distinction is tested directly in your exam.
  • Both are social constructs: what counts as criminal or deviant varies across time (historical variation), place (cultural variation) and social situation, showing that these categories are created by society rather than fixed by nature.
  • Functionalists, Marxists, feminists and interactionists each offer a different explanation for who defines crime and deviance and whose interests those definitions serve.

practice_questions.text:
Which of the following is the best sociological definition of deviance?
A) An act that breaks the criminal law
B) Any behaviour that violates the social norms of a group or society
C) Behaviour that is harmful to other people
D) An act that results in a formal state punishment
practice_questions.marks: B) Any behaviour that violates the social norms of a group or society [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Define what sociologists mean by the term 'social construct'.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying that a social construct is something created or defined by people in society rather than existing naturally or objectively. 1 mark for developing this: e.g. it varies across time, place or culture, so it is not fixed or universal. Full answer: a category or concept that is created and defined by people in society rather than being natural or objective, and which may change over time or differ between cultures.

practice_questions.text: Identify and describe one way in which the definition of crime has changed over time in England and Wales.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying an act whose legal status has changed over time (e.g. fox hunting with dogs; consensual sexual activity between adult men; marital rape). 2 marks for a developed description: explaining what the law was before, what it became and when the change occurred. Example: fox hunting with dogs was a lawful activity in England and Wales until the Hunting Act 2004 made it a criminal offence, demonstrating that the definition of crime is not fixed but shaped by changing social values and the exercise of political power.

practice_questions.text: Describe how two different sociological perspectives explain the social construction of crime.
practice_questions.marks: 2 marks per perspective. 1 mark for identifying the perspective's basic position; 1 mark for developing it with a named concept or sociologist. Acceptable pairs: Functionalist (crime defined by value consensus; Durkheim on boundary maintenance) + Marxist (law serves ruling-class/bourgeoisie interests, criminalises working-class acts while ignoring white-collar crime). Or: Feminist (law has historically encoded patriarchal values, e.g. late criminalisation of marital rape) + Interactionist (Becker's labelling theory, moral entrepreneurs, no act inherently criminal).

practice_questions.text: Discuss the view that what counts as criminal or deviant is shaped entirely by those with power in society.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Both sides of the debate addressed with named sociologists and sustained sociological vocabulary. In support: Marxist argument that the bourgeoisie shape the law to protect property and criminalise working-class behaviour; feminist argument that patriarchal power historically excluded harms against women from legal definition (e.g. marital rape); interactionist argument (Becker) that moral entrepreneurs with social power drive the labelling of certain acts as criminal. Qualifying or against: Functionalist view that crime is defined by value consensus reflecting the whole community's shared morality, not just elite interests; Durkheim's boundary maintenance function suggests legal definitions can serve broader social needs. Student cites at least two named sociologists, presents both sides, and reaches a supported judgement. Secure: Both sides covered, named sociologists present, judgement reached. Developing: One-sided or underdeveloped, some named theorists, conclusion assertive. Emerging: Basic descriptive points, few named sociologists, little evaluative judgement.

practice_questions.text: Evaluate the claim that crime and deviance are always relative to the social context in which they occur.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Full range of relevant arguments for and against with at least two named sociologists or perspectives developed in detail, sustained sociological vocabulary, and a clear supported judgement. For the claim: interactionist evidence (Becker, Outsiders 1963) that deviance is not a quality of the act itself but is created by social reactions; historical variation (fox hunting, decriminalisation of consensual same-sex acts); cultural variation (alcohol, cannabis across jurisdictions); situational variation (self-defence vs murder). Against or qualifying: functionalist view that some acts (e.g. serious violence against persons) are universally condemned across cultures, suggesting a degree of universal moral consensus; Durkheim's value consensus implies stable moral boundaries, not pure relativism. Student weighs both sides and reaches a clear judgement about the extent to which relativism holds. Secure: Most relevant arguments present, both sides covered, named sociologists referenced, judgement reached. Developing: Relevant points but mostly one-sided or undeveloped, some theorists named, conclusion assertive. Emerging: Basic points, mostly description, few named sociologists, little judgement.

knowledge_checks.q: Which of the following is an example of an act that is criminal but NOT widely considered deviant?
options: Committing a violent assault on a stranger
Slightly exceeding the speed limit on a motorway
Wearing pyjamas to a formal dinner

knowledge_checks.q: Which sociological perspective argues that criminal law primarily reflects and protects the interests of the bourgeoisie?
Behaviour that violates social norms, whether or not it is illegal, is called _____.
According to Becker, people who campaign to get behaviours defined as deviant or criminal are called _____ entrepreneurs.
Match each perspective to its explanation of how crime is socially constructed:
right: Crime is defined by shared social values and norms of the community
Law is shaped by the ruling class to protect their property and power
An act becomes deviant only when others successfully label it as such

flashcard_questions.q: What is the sociological definition of deviance?
flashcard_questions.a: Any behaviour that violates the social norms of a group or society, whether or not it is illegal.

flashcard_questions.q: What is the sociological definition of crime?
flashcard_questions.a: An act that breaks the formal law of a society and may result in a state-imposed punishment.
A category or concept created and defined by people in society rather than existing naturally or objectively.

flashcard_questions.q: Give one example of an act that is deviant but not criminal.
flashcard_questions.a: Queue-jumping — it violates social norms but breaks no law and carries no legal penalty.

flashcard_questions.q: Give one example of an act that is criminal but not widely seen as deviant.
flashcard_questions.a: Minor speeding — many motorists exceed the limit slightly but do not consider themselves criminals.

flashcard_questions.q: What are moral entrepreneurs, according to Becker?
flashcard_questions.a: People or groups who campaign to get certain behaviours defined as deviant or criminal.

flashcard_questions.q: How does the Marxist perspective explain who defines crime?
flashcard_questions.a: The bourgeoisie shape the law to protect their interests, criminalising working-class acts while protecting elite behaviour.

flashcard_questions.q: How does the feminist perspective critique the social construction of crime?
flashcard_questions.a: Laws were historically made by men and encoded patriarchal values, failing to criminalise harms against women.

flashcard_questions.q: What is the functionalist view of why crime is defined by society?
flashcard_questions.a: Crime is defined by value consensus — laws express the community's shared moral boundaries.
Rewards or punishments used to encourage conformity to social norms or rules.

flashcard_questions.q: Give an example of how the definition of crime varies across time.
flashcard_questions.a: Fox hunting with dogs was lawful in England and Wales until the Hunting Act 2004 made it criminal.

flashcard_questions.q: Give an example of how the definition of crime varies across place.
flashcard_questions.a: Cannabis possession is permitted under certain conditions in the Netherlands but is a criminal offence in England and Wales.

glossary_terms.definition: An act that breaks the formal law of a society and may result in a state-imposed punishment such as a fine or imprisonment.
Any behaviour that violates the social norms of a group or society, whether or not it is illegal.
A category or concept created and defined by people in society rather than existing as a natural or objective fact; it can change over time and across cultures.
Shared, largely unwritten expectations about how people should behave in a given social situation.
Rewards or punishments used to encourage conformity to norms or rules; positive sanctions reward conformity, negative sanctions punish deviation.
People or groups in positions of influence who campaign to have certain behaviours defined as deviant or criminal and brought under social control.
The shared beliefs and values that, according to functionalist theory, bind society together and provide the basis for defining acceptable behaviour.
In Marxist theory, the class that owns the means of production and uses its economic and political power to shape laws and institutions in its own interests.
